title: FICCI Puts Air Pollution's Annual Cost at $95 Billion, Urges Health-Led Plan
headline: FICCI Puts Air Pollution's Annual Cost at $95 Billion, Urges Health-Led Plan
subheadline: A FICCI-EY paper links polluted air to more than two million deaths in India in 2023 and calls for explicit PM2.5 targets, regional airshed action and year-round health planning instead of seasonal emergency responses.
summary: A FICCI-EY paper links polluted air to more than two million deaths in India in 2023 and calls for explicit PM2.5 targets, regional airshed action and year-round health planning instead of seasonal emergency responses.
excerpt: A FICCI-EY paper links polluted air to more than two million deaths in India in 2023 and calls for explicit PM2.5 targets, regional airshed action and year-round health planning instead of seasonal emergency responses.
body:
• Air pollution was attributable to more than two million deaths in India in 2023, according to the FICCI-EY knowledge paper 'Clean Air, Healthy India'.
  • The paper puts annual economic losses as high as $95 billion, about 3% of GDP, with roughly 1.3 billion working days lost each year.
  • More than 660 million Indians live in areas where fine particulate (PM2.5) pollution exceeds national safety standards, and exposure is estimated to cut average life expectancy by about 3.5 years.
  • For anyone in India this winter, or flying in to visit family: the paper's central warning is that polluted air is a year-round health risk, not a seasonal one — check the local AQI before planning outdoor time on high-pollution days.

The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) has put a price on India's dirty air. In a 76-page knowledge paper prepared with EY and released on November 5, the industry body estimates air pollution-related losses could run as high as $95 billion a year, about 3% of GDP, and argues that clean air must move to the centre of India's healthcare agenda instead of being treated as a seasonal environmental problem.

The paper, titled 'Clean Air, Healthy India', lands days after Diwali, when several of New Delhi's air quality monitors went silent at the peak of the smog season, according to NDTV's report on the study. FICCI represents more than 2.5 lakh companies, and a warning of this tone from the country's industry lobby carries a different weight than the usual winter commentary.

The health toll the paper lays out

More than two million deaths in India in 2023 were attributable to air pollution, the paper says. More than 660 million people live in areas where PM2.5 levels exceed national safety standards, and long-term exposure is estimated to shorten the average Indian's life expectancy by about 3.5 years. NDTV's coverage of the report adds that 99 of the world's 100 most polluted cities are in India and that nearly a billion Indians breathe toxic air.

The paper treats PM2.5 as a whole-body risk rather than only a lung problem: the particles can penetrate deep into the lungs, enter the bloodstream and affect nearly every organ system. Long-term exposure is linked to asthma and chronic lung disease, but also to heart attacks, stroke, heart failure, neurological disorders, cognitive decline, dementia risk and adverse pregnancy outcomes. The burden falls hardest on children, the elderly, outdoor workers, low-income communities and people who already have respiratory or cardiovascular illness.

What dirty air costs the economy

The economic case rests on lost work, reduced output, healthcare spending and premature deaths. About 1.3 billion working days are lost annually, the paper estimates, and productivity can decline by 8% to 10% during heavily polluted periods. Put together, the authors arrive at losses of up to $95 billion a year.

"Clean air must be central to India's healthcare agenda, not treated solely as an environmental objective."

— Dr Ashutosh Raghuvanshi, Chair, FICCI Health Services Committee and MD & CEO, Fortis Healthcare

Dr Raghuvanshi, speaking for the FICCI-EY paper, said healthcare institutions have a role in raising awareness, tracking pollution-related illness and improving preparedness, and called for closer collaboration between government, industry and healthcare providers so clean-air commitments translate into measurable public health improvements. Dr Arun Agarwal, who chairs FICCI's Working Group on Air Pollution, argued India must move beyond seasonal responses that focus only on winter smog episodes, with exposure reduction treated as a year-round public health priority.

Why Delhi cannot fix Delhi alone

One of the paper's sharpest findings concerns geography. Local sources account for only about 36% of Delhi's PM2.5 pollution in winter and about 26% in summer; the rest drifts in from outside the city limits. On those numbers, city-by-city action cannot work, and the paper calls for a comprehensive 'airshed' approach that manages pollution across the regions it actually moves through.

FICCI says existing responses — the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), Bharat Stage emission norms and clean cooking initiatives — have delivered some benefits but remain fragmented and largely reactive.

What FICCI wants changed

The paper's central recommendation is a change in what gets measured. NCAP currently relies heavily on PM10 levels, while PM2.5 is the more dangerous pollutant for health; FICCI wants explicit PM2.5 reduction targets written into the programme, expanded monitoring, and public health indicators tied directly to pollution reduction. Its ten practical solutions include closed-loop dust control at construction sites, hyperlocal monitoring networks, smart traffic systems to cut congestion, cleaner industrial technologies, cleaner brick kilns, replacing diesel generators with battery-based systems, turning crop residue into useful products instead of burning it, and circular use of waste in construction. The full paper is published by EY.

The recommendations are advisory; whether NCAP gains binding PM2.5 targets is now a decision for the government. Until then, the paper's practical message for readers is the one in its title: treat clean air as a health issue every month of the year, not an emergency that begins with the first smog headline.
